newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RAND MAY FORCE LOCAL COAL PRICE UP - AMCOAL. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: RAND MAY FORCE LOCAL COAL PRICE UP - AMCOAL. [CORRECTED 16:00 GMT]

text.p: South Africa's domestic coal prices will suffer continued upward pressure due to the rand's slide against the dollar which has widened the gap between export and domestic prices, Anglo American Coal Corp said.

Speaking at a presentation of the group's interim results, Amcoal marketing director Hugh Stacey (corrects name) said: "The major weakening in the rand since February this year has widened considerably the gap between export and domestic prices and this will lead to continued upward pressure on prices in the domestic market."
The rand has lost more than 30 percent of its value against the dollar since mid-February and was last bid at 4.7075.
As a result, Amcoal was looking into developing additional capacity for the local market, Stacey said.

"Amcoal is currently examining on a preliminary basis the possible development of additional capacity targeted primarily at the local market and increased price levels are important in justifying the necessary investment," he said.
Amcoal highlighted its current Bank Colliery expansion project which was expected to bring on an additional 600,000 tonnes per annum of production.
The Bank project is expected to reach full production by the end of fiscal 1997 and is seen costing about 140 million rand, Amcoal said.
"We look at local demand and believe we can get more tonnes to the local sector," Amcoal chairman David Rankin said.
Amcoal posted earnings per share for the six months ended September 30 of 1,680.4 cents versus 1,283.6 cents previously. It declared a dividend of 420 cents per share compared to 300.

Turning to current pricing negotiations, Amcoal said spot prices were currently above contract prices, showing a robust framework in which to pursue contract pricing for 1997. "We are in a reasonably firm position for next year," Amcoal said.
The group said that a weak point in the coal market was Australia where there was an abundance of spot coal. But it added that the abundance was unlikely to impact too severely.
Amcoal said 1996 exports through the Richards Bay Coal Terminal were unlikely to match those of last year and would likely range between 58 and 59 million tonnes.
Richards Bay is expected to reach its 63 million tonne capacity by the end of March 1997 and Amcoal said it planned to utilise any increased capacity offered by the terminal.

"Amcoal is planning to take advantage of the progressive commsioning of Richards Bay's additional capacity. We are planning to obviously take up our full share of Richards Bay at 63 million," Rankin said.

But he also emphasised that no decision had yet been taken by Richards Bay on further expansion which could take capacity to around 67 million tonnes. Rankin forecast Richards Bay's 1997 tonnage at 62 million tonnes.

Amcoal said it was investigating overseas investments but that a major criterion was that the investment offer more value than its current cash position. As yet the group hs not identified any such possible venture.
Turning to costs, Amcoal said that the decline in the rand was starting to impact on some of the group's imports.
Amcoal currently held no forward sales positions.
